transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-01-12
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~1h15m
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Sam Carter (CTO - Aurelius), Lina Rodriguez (Platform Eng), Devon Kim (Ops)

Summary:
Redwood SE-led deep dive on Private VPC deployment networking and runtime implications. Covered PrivateLink vs VPC peering, NAT and egress, subnet sizing, DNS (private zones), and runtime performance knobs (KV cache, batching, quant, kernel selection). Action items to share design artifacts and schedule benchmarks.

Topics:
- PrivateLink architecture and connectivity patterns
- NAT/egress and static IPs for allowlists
- Subnet design and IP planning for GPU nodes
- DNS/private hosted zones and split-horizon configs
- Runtime performance: KV cache warmup, batching, sequence lengths, quantization tradeoffs
- Fall-back strategies and monitoring

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: all right hey everyone thanks for hopping on. quick intros  im maya, account lead for aurelius. ethan's our SE, he'll drive the tech deep dive.
[00:12] Ethan: hey hi, morning  uh  afternoon all. quick agenda, we'll talk connectivity options first private link vs peering, then runtime perf implications, and finish with a proposed pilot and benchmarks. sound good?
[00:25] Sam: yep sounds good, thanks. our main constraints are compliance  we need traffic to stay in our VPC and egress IPs to be static for our partner allowlists. latency target is p99 < 120ms for our customer-facing route. cost is also a factor.
[00:40] Ethan: great, good constraints to call out. quick caveat  some transcription may be off, i might say KV "cash" or things like that, but uh it's KV cache.
[00:48] Lina: noted. can you start with private link? we've got questions on routing and how traffic flows to your runtime.
[00:55] Ethan: sure. so PrivateLink  in our recommended setup Redwood runs a private NLB per-customer in our control plane region and exposes an interface endpoint in your VPC. that means connections terminate over AWS' ENIs and traffic doesn't traverse the public internet. pros: no public IPs, easier allowlist. cons: you need an interface endpoint in each AZ you want low cross-AZ traffic  also there are per-ENI IP requirements.
[01:18] Devon: so do we need to open any outbound NAT to talk to your control plane?
[01:22] Ethan: depends  control plane calls for metrics/health check callbacks sometimes go outbound, but for inference path if you use PrivateLink it can be purely inbound (from your VPC to our NLB via the interface endpoint). however if you plan to use our managed autoscaling control plane or updates, you might see egress to Redwood management endpoints; we can also support a private control plane in our Private offering.
[01:40] Sam: what's the alternative? VPC peering?
[01:43] Ethan: VPC peering is an option but it has limitations: peering across accounts/regions requires route tables and doesn't support transitive routing, and you'd need to manage peering per region. PrivateLink is usually cleaner for SaaS-style connectivity. For on-prem we also support VPN or Direct Connect.
[02:00] Lina: subnet sizing  for GPU nodes we want dedicated subnets with /26 or /27? what's best practice?
[02:06] Ethan: for GPU instances you need multiple IPs per node sometimes (ENI + pods if using k8s). in most of our Private deployments customers use /24 per GPU subnet in large clusters to avoid hitting ENI limits, but for PrivateLink interface endpoints the ENI consumes 1 IP per AZ per endpoint. if you have tight IP address space we can do NAT plus port mapping but that complicates allowlists.
[02:30] Sam: ok that helps. what about NAT and static egress IPs  we need fixed egress for partner APIs.
[02:36] Ethan: we recommend using NAT Gateway with Elastic IPs or egress NAT instances. for pilot we can provide a small range of egress IPs you can allowlist; for production we also support routing via customer-managed NAT and we can document the IP ranges. if you need absolute static dedicated IPs per node that's possible with networking appliances but more ops overhead.
[02:55] Devon: and DNS? we run Route 53 private hosted zones, split-horizon for internal services. any pitfalls?
[03:00] Ethan: Route53 private zones are fine. main pitfall is DNS resolution for the interface endpoint  make sure the VPC resolver is allowed and your private zone doesn't shadow the endpoint domain names. we typically recommend creating a private hosted zone for redwood.example.local that points to the interface endpoint IPs, or using the default interface endpoint DNS name that AWS auto-registers. also watch TTLs during failover.
[03:24] Lina: got it. switching to runtime  latency. our critical path is short prompts with high QPS, p99 < 120ms. what levers do we have?
[03:33] Ethan: there are a few layers. first, model selection and sequence length distribution  shorter sequences, less KV cache pressure. second, batching: we can do adaptive batching with tight latency SLOs, but batching increases tail latency if you wait too long for a batch to fill. we tune batch windows. third, KV cache locality: for chat use cases with long conv history we rely on KV cache to avoid recomputing prefixes; warm cache to reduce repeated context cost. fourth, quantization: int8 or 4-bit quant reduces GPU memory and can improve throughput, but might slightly degrade quality on edge cases.
[04:05] Sam: can you quantify expected p99 impact from enabling KV cache?
[04:09] Ethan: roughly, warm KV cache can cut p99 by 20-50% depending on how much prefix reuse you have. example: a 2048-token conv where 80% of tokens are from a cached prefix  on that pattern we've seen p99 drop from ~300ms to ~110-140ms on T4-like instances. for A100 or H100 it's faster. caveat: those numbers vary by model size and hardware; we'll run lab benchmarks with your payloads.
[04:38] Lina: about batching, what's your recommendation at high QPS?
[04:42] Ethan: use adaptive batching with two knobs: max latency window (say 5-10ms for low-tail) and max batch size. For your latency SLO I'd start with 5ms window, that keeps p99 low while still giving ~20-30% throughput improvement. If cost becomes critical we can relax window to 10-15ms.
[04:59] Devon: quantization  do you do quant-aware kernels? any compatibility issues?
[05:03] Ethan: yes, our runtime has quantized execution paths and kernel selection  we pick kernels based on model, sequence length, and hardware. we support 8-bit and 4-bit quant on supported models; we also keep a float fallback for critical calls. common gotcha: some community models lose a bit of instruction-following performance at 4-bit; we recommend a quality eval on your prompts.
[05:24] Maya: quick note  we'll share a quantization recommendation matrix per model after this call.
[05:29] Sam: monitoring  how do we get p99 and per-token cost visibility?
[05:32] Ethan: Redwood Console exposes per-route latency, p50/p95/p99, token counts, and model-level cost estimates. For Private we can ship a metrics collector to your monitoring stack (Prometheus/Grafana) or expose metrics over CloudWatch.
[05:46] Lina: failure modes  if interface endpoint goes down or a region has issue how do you failover?
[05:51] Ethan: we support multi-AZ endpoints and multi-region fallbacks. we recommend a primary PrivateLink endpoint and a secondary in another AZ/region with routing at your side. for cross-region we can route to a compatible model variant and degrade performance gracefully. we'll document DNS TTLs and healthcheck settings.
[06:06] Sam: are there any compliance concerns with PrivateLink?
[06:09] Ethan: PrivateLink actually helps with compliance by avoiding public traffic. we also provide audit logs, KMS integrations, and can run in a customer-managed control plane for stricter requirements  that'll be part of our Private offering contract.
[06:20] Devon: quick question on IP exhaustion  you mentioned ENIs per endpoint  how many IPs should we reserve?
[06:25] Ethan: rule of thumb: each interface endpoint can consume 1-3 IPs per AZ depending on throughput. if you plan to use one endpoint per AZ and have multiple services, reserve at least /28 per AZ for endpoints plus the IPs for GPU subnets. if you have limited address space, we can design an architecture that uses fewer endpoints and NAT for outbound flows.
[06:44] Lina: ok good. pilot proposal?
[06:46] Ethan: pilot we propose: one PrivateLink endpoint in two AZs, small dedicated GPU pool (2-4 nodes) with /24 subnets, NAT gateway with 2 Elastic IPs for egress, and a baseline benchmark run including KV cache warmup pattern and simulated QPS. we'll capture p50/p95/p99, token cost, and CPU/GPU utilization.
[07:05] Sam: timeline?
[07:07] Maya: if we get the VPC details this week we can stand up the pilot next week and run benchmarks the following week  so kickoff week of 2026-01-26.
[07:15] Lina: sounds good, we'll send CIDRs and DNS details by Monday.
[07:20] Ethan: perfect. i'll follow up with the CF/Terraform snippet and a benchmark plan.
[07:24] Maya: recap  redwood to share PrivateLink diagram + CF, latency benchmark plan, SOC2/ISO summary; aurelius to share VPC CIDRs, NAT/eip requirements, and DNS config. action items in the notes. thanks everyone.
[07:36] Sam: thanks, really useful.

End of call.
